Q43089790.summary: Carved from a single piece of ivory, this comb has a fine row of teeth below an openwork field showing Christ on the cross, with a small titulus above, the Virgin and Saint John beside him and the soldiers with lance and sponge kneeling at the foot; half-length figures appear above the arms of the cross. Rosettes of openwork and curling acanthus fill the sides, and two figures bend among the scrolls at the top. Such combs were used in the liturgy, so that even a preparation for worship was set under the sign of the cross.
facts: The Museum Schnütgen holds the comb as inventory B 100; it is traditionally associated with Saint Heribert, Archbishop of Cologne (died 1021), though it was made more than a century before his time.

Liturgical combs of the 9th and 10th centuries were usually carved from a single piece of ivory and decorated with religious scenes, unlike secular combs; their exact use, perhaps at a bishop's consecration or before Mass, is unclear.
Q43089790.notes: Date and place (Metz, 850–900) come from the museum label as recorded in the Commons file title. Heribert's dates are general knowledge. The upper figures were not identified.

cur:catacombs-arles-orante-frieze.summary: A praying woman with raised arms stands at the centre of a crowded frieze in which Christ performs miracles among the apostles. The orans – the image of the soul in prayer – is placed literally in the midst of Christ's saving acts.
facts: The museum calls it the 'Sarcophage de l'Orante'.
Arles possesses the largest collection of early Christian sarcophagi outside Rome.
cur:catacombs-arles-orante-frieze.notes: Date approximate; individual scenes not verified.

vam:O92728.summary: This long, narrow ivory strip tells the story of Christ's birth as one continuous frieze: the Magi in Phrygian caps see the star and set out, the Christ Child lies in a manger in an open shed with the ox and the ass while Mary sits beside him, and further on the Magi hurry forward with their gifts to the Child held on his mother's lap. Rather than dividing the episodes, the carver lets them flow into one another, as on late-antique caskets.
facts: The panel is one of three in the V&A from a casket that was formerly in the Abbey of Werden in Westphalia; they were purchased from the Webb collection in 1866.
Scholars remain divided over whether the panels are Early Christian or Carolingian copies of Early Christian (perhaps 5th-century) models; the V&A favours a date of about 800.
The V&A links the group stylistically to a book cover in the treasury of Milan Cathedral and to related panels in Berlin, Toulouse and Nevers.
vam:O92728.notes: The V&A qualifies place and date with 'probably' (probably Lower Rhine, probably Werden, probably ca. 800).
